name: Through Iowa: Notes from the Maintenance Window
author: Yalena Nakamura-Svensson, independent freight driver
description: A first-person account from a freight driver who transited Iowa during the annual Behemoth maintenance cycle, describing the machines, the silence, and the towns that serve them.
body:
I drove through Iowa during the maintenance window because the routing fee was forty percent lower and I needed the money. The GLMZ freight brokers who know Iowa told me what to expect, and I'll tell you what they told me, and then I'll tell you what I actually found, and you can decide how useful the advance information was.

What I was told: the Iowan Behemoths are agricultural automation units, operated by the Iowa Agro-Compact since roughly 2140, with no human equivalent for scale or function. Each unit manages between forty and eighty thousand hectares of farmland autonomously — planting, irrigation, harvest, soil management, pest response, the whole chain. There are between sixty and ninety of them active at any given time, and they are very large. The maintenance window runs six weeks every September and October, when a rotating third of the fleet pauses in place for diagnostic cycles. During the window, certain transit corridors open because the machines that normally cross them are stationary.

All of that is accurate. What I was not told is what it feels like.

The first thing you notice when you cross into Iowa from the Illinois side is that the scale is wrong. Not wrong as in broken — wrong as in your spatial intuition is calibrated for GLMZ and it stops working. I am used to vertical density. Iowa is horizontal density. The fields go to the horizon in every direction and they are not separate fields — they are continuous, managed, a single vast organism of cultivated land that the Behemoths tend the way a gardener tends a garden, except the gardener is seven stories tall and does not distinguish between you and the weeds.

I saw my first Behemoth parked about forty kilometers west of the Illinois line, just off the N7 transit corridor — one of the approved routes during the window. It was in a harvested cornfield, powered down, and it was enormous. I stopped the truck because I needed to understand the scale before I continued. I had seen photographs. Photographs do not communicate the thing in the field about four hundred meters from where you are standing, motionless, rust-colored, the size of a large building lying on its side, with six articulated harvest arms folded along its body like the legs of a sleeping insect. It was not running. It was not making any sound I could detect. It did not react to me in any way. And yet I sat there for eleven minutes before I felt it was safe to continue.

The towns between the machine-farms are real and they are inhabited. The people in them are focused in a way that I can only describe as purposeful narrowness. They are not unfriendly. They answer questions. They sell fuel, food, basic supplies. They do not ask what you're carrying and they do not ask where you're going. The Behemoths require servicing that the machines cannot do themselves — fluid replenishment, certain mechanical calibrations, sensor cleaning, electrical system access during diagnostic cycles. The towns do this. That is, as far as I could determine, the organizing principle of their economy.

In a town called Harlan — maybe three thousand people, a main street, a repair depot that looked like it could service something the size of a building — I ate at a diner and talked with the woman behind the counter for about twenty minutes. She had the focused practicality of someone who has worked a demanding job for thirty years and has no patience for anything that does not bear directly on the work. I asked her what it was like living with the Behemoths and she looked at me with an expression that I can only describe as the look you give someone who has asked what it's like living with weather.

'They need what they need,' she said. 'We provide it. That's the arrangement.'

I asked if the arrangement had always been that way. She said her grandmother remembered the transition, when the Compact phased out the last human farm workers. I asked if there was resentment about that. She thought about it for what felt like a genuine thinking pause and then said, 'My grandmother was a farm worker. She had bad knees and a bad back and she worked until she couldn't. I run diagnostics and calibrate sensors and I have good knees. Which of us had the worse deal?'

I did not have an answer. I drove out of Harlan and back into the fields.

The last thing I'll say: during the maintenance window, when the machines are stationary, Iowa is the quietest place I have ever been. Not countryside-quiet. Not night-quiet. Something else. The silence of enormous purpose temporarily paused. The sensation that the stillness is not natural but held — that the machines are not off, just resting, and that the resting is a kind of breathing. I am describing a feeling, not a fact. The machines are machines. But I drove through Iowa as fast as the corridors allowed and I was glad when Illinois came back.
